Removal methods

Three ways we get bees out

The right method depends on where the colony is living. Every removal ends with the bees in a new home — and the opening sealed so they can't return.

Cut-Outs

Our preferred method. We locate the colony with inspection and infrared cameras, open the cavity — eaves, soffits, walls, floors or ceilings — vacuum the bees gently, remove all wax and comb, then seal the openings.

Trap-Outs

For colonies that can't be reached by cut-out — inside a block wall or a tree. A one-way trap lets bees leave but not return, guiding them into a new hive over several weeks.

Swarm Removal

Each spring, colonies swarm and cluster on branches while scouts hunt for a new home. That's the ideal moment to call — before they move into your walls. Swarm removals within 30 miles of Sandersville or Dublin: call Karen Palmer.

Why rescue matters

A colony is worth saving

A single colony holds 30,000 to 60,000 honeybees, hard at work. Left in a wall, they'll build pound after pound of honey-filled comb — and if a colony is poisoned instead of removed, the leftover honey melts, seeps into the structure and draws roaches, mice and other pests. Removing the bees, the comb and the honey solves the whole problem — and gives the colony a new home.

Before we come out

What we'll ask you

  • Where are the bees entering the structure?
  • When did you first notice them?
  • About how high is the entry point?
  • Can you send a photo, so we can plan access?
